Do the following using the steps provided in their respective sections.
        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis. 
            2.2 kubernetes yamls based on the analysis.
            2.3 github actions file to build application on pushing to main branch.
        3. add all changed file to git changes 
        4. commit / push to repo

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt into a script) to accomplish everything you asked for.  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, give you the exact shell commands, and show you the files that will be generated.  
Feel free to tweak the defaults (e.g., base image, replicas, etc.) to match your own conventions.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re on Windows and don’t have an SSH key yet, run `ssh-keygen` and add the public key to your GitHub account first.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Analyse the predominant language

```bash
# Install the `linguist` gem if you want a quick local check
gem install linguist

# Run Linguist to see the language breakdown
linguist --json . > linguist_report.json
```

Open `linguist_report.json` and look for the `"languages"` field.  
If Node.js (JavaScript/TypeScript) dominates, you’re good to go.  
If another language is predominant, adjust the defaults below accordingly.

> **Quick sanity check** – You can also just eyeball the repo: if most files end in `.js`, `.ts`, or `.jsx`, it’s almost certainly a Node.js project.

### 2.2 Create a Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# Use the official lightweight Node.js runtime
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
LABEL description="Node.js app built from zelars welcome template"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:20-alpine` is small, secure, and includes the latest LTS Node.js.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the typical port used in the repo’s `package.json`.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (create the `k8s` folder if it doesn’t exist):

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2          # Adjust as needed
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # Replace with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer     # Change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys two replicas (adjust `replicas:`).  
> * Exposes the app via a LoadBalancer (use `NodePort` if you’re on bare metal).  
> * Maps external port 80 → internal port 3000.

### 2.4 Add a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **How it works**  
> * Triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Builds the image using the Dockerfile in the repo root.  
> * Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry under the same name as the repo (`ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome`).  
> * Uses the automatically provided `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` for authentication.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

> If you want to stage *everything* that was changed (including any other modifications you made), you can simply run `git add .` instead.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will fire automatically (if you’re on the `main` branch).  
> Check the Actions tab on GitHub to confirm the build succeeded.

---

### Quick sanity checks after the push

1. **Verify the Docker image**  
   ```bash
   docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
   ```

2. **Deploy locally with Minikube or Kind**  
   ```bash
   kind load docker-image ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
   kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
   ```

3. **Check the service**  
   ```bash
   kubectl get svc nodejs-welcome-service
   ```

---

That’s it!  
You now have a fully working CI pipeline that builds a Docker image on every push to `main`, and you’ve got ready‑to‑apply Kubernetes manifests that will spin up two replicas behind a LoadBalancer.  

Happy coding!
